newsitem.title: UK: Charts, fundamentals both favour Europe bond bulls.
newsitem.headline: Charts, fundamentals both favour Europe bond bulls.

text.p: Economists and technicians have called a truce over Europe's debt markets, with both predicting a steady climb in prices to the end of the year.
Their methods are wildly different, but their conclusions are the same. So asset allocators can be reassured by this rare united front after a recently stalled bull run.

Craig Shute, fixed income analyst at Bear Stearns in London, said the medium-term technical and fundamental outlook for Bunds, the main engine of European debt markets, was pointing in the same direction -- up.
"The outlook for the Bund market remains constructive," he said.

"From a fundamental view, the recovery is underway in Germany but it's weak and anaemic and to guarantee success there will have to be more interest rate cuts from the Bundesbank," Shute said. "We're not looking for investor angst on inflationary worries in Germany."
Ten-year Bund yields have had trouble making a sustained break below 6.0 percent, and have been largely confined to a 6.0 percent to 6.5 percent trading range since February.
"We think the Bund can get to this year's low of 5.78 percent within a three-month time frame," Shute said.
Technical analysts agreed the bull run was yet to run out of steam.
Robin Wilkin, senior technical analyst at MCM Yieldwatch, said the market would rally convincingly if the December futures contract managed to close above 100.00 in the near term.
By 1441 GMT on Friday the contract was trading at 99.79 on LIFFE, 19 basis points above Thursday's close, after getting a boost from October U.S. payrolls data in line with expectations.
"If we close above 100.00, it's going to rally quite quickly to 101-36, which is the high on January 28, according to continuation charts," Wilkin said.

"If the bull trend continues, we're looking at 102.85 over the next seven months or so...which is the initial Fibonacci projection level." But he did caution a close near lows on Friday lent a more bearish tone to the market, especially if support at 99.02 was broken.
Market watchers are split on the reliability of technical analysis versus fundamentals in predicting future market moves.
Die-hard technicians rely on esoterically named patterns such as evening stars, black crows, dead crosses and pennants to determine price direction.
But economists are loyal to the more traditional indicators of economic growth and inflationary pressures such as labour market and gross domestic product data.
Philip Gardiner, fixed income analyst at Technical Data, was particularly bullish on the outlook for Bunds.
Bunds have been in an upward trend since June.
"The initial target comes in at 100.72 and above there, if the bull trend has resumed, a straight projection comes in at 101.95/102.00," Gardiner said.

He added by the end of the year Bund futures could be as high as 104.00 or 105.00. But with European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) the buzz word in Europe's markets at present, fundamentalists argue bonds are increasingly at the mercy of politicians, not charts. "Almost all fundamental news overwrites technical news," Gardiner said. "Fundamentals will move the market and techncials will predict the direction."
So much for the truce.
